## What was wrong

`docs/IMPROVEMENTS.md` item 11: `dashboard/tabs/prices.py`'s `save_price_history_changes()` was 40% covered and had the same falsy-zero bug already fixed once in the Products editor (`dashboard.saves.to_price`/`_differs`):

- **Add guard** `if pd.isna(price) or not price` treated a 0.00 TND price (a free sample, a giveaway) as missing — the row was silently never added, no error shown.
- **Edit coercion** `float(v) if pd.notna(v) and v else None` coerced an edited 0.00 to `None`. `price_tnd` is `nullable=False` at the DB level, so this does **not** silently null the value as the backlog item suspected — it raises `IntegrityError` on `db.commit()`, and because every row in the editor is saved under one commit, it rolled back **every other edit in the same save**, not just the zero-priced row. Proven in `test_regression_unfixed_coercion_corrupts_the_whole_batch` by reverting the fix and watching a sibling row's genuine edit disappear too.
- The adjacent change-detection line, `str(new or "") != str(old or "")`, collapses `0.0`/`""`/`None` to the same `""`, so even with the cast fixed, a price set to exactly 0.00 could still read as "no change" and never reach `db.commit`. Fixed alongside.
- The manual "Add a price record" form had the identical `pr_price:` truthy guard; fixed to `pr_price is not None`.

## What changed

- `price = to_price(row.get("price_tnd"))` (add path) and `new_val = to_price(new_val)` (edit path) reuse `dashboard.saves.to_price` instead of duplicating the buggy inline casts.
- New `_changed(old_val, new_val)` helper, mirroring `dashboard.saves._differs`, replaces the falsy-collapsing string comparison.
- Manual-add-form guard: `pr_price is not None` instead of `pr_price`.

## How I checked it

- Reverted the fix and confirmed `test_zero_price_record_is_added_not_skipped`, `test_price_edited_to_zero_is_persisted`, `test_editing_one_row_to_zero_does_not_roll_back_a_sibling_edit` and `test_regression_unfixed_coercion_corrupts_the_whole_batch` all **fail** against the old code, then restored it and confirmed all 18 new tests pass.
- `./venv/bin/pytest -q`: **644 passed** (was 626).
- `./venv/bin/ruff check .`: clean.
- Coverage of `dashboard/tabs/prices.py`: 40% → 77%.

## What was not covered

The manual "Add a price record" form's Streamlit body itself is not driven through `AppTest` in this PR — its fix (the truthy-guard change) is exercised only by inspection and by the same `_changed`/`to_price` unit tests, not by simulating a form submission. The chart-rendering branches of the tab remain untested (not a write path).

## Backlog

Item 11 struck through and closed out in `docs/IMPROVEMENTS.md`, with a correction to the backlog's own description of the edit-coercion bug (batch-corrupting `IntegrityError`, not a silent null).

## What changed
Backlog item 8b. `src/reporters/email_sender.py` was at 19% coverage — only
its `__init__` and module-level imports were exercised by anything else in
the suite. Added `tests/test_email_sender.py` (15 tests) mocking
`smtplib.SMTP` and the TLS handshake throughout; no real network or SMTP
server is touched by any test.

Covers:
- The recipients-required guard on both `send_notification` and `send_report`
- TLS handshake order (`ehlo` → `starttls` → `ehlo` → `login`), and that
  `login` is skipped when no credentials are configured
- `send_report`'s PDF-attach failure path fails closed without sending
- Generated vs. caller-supplied subject/body
- `test_connection` success and failure

No production code changed.

## Why
Every send path in this module (notification alerts, the weekly PDF report
delivery) was unverified. A broken SMTP call, a missing-recipients guard, or
a bad PDF attach would only be discovered in production — silently killing
an alert or the weekly report.

## Verified
- `./venv/bin/pytest -q`: 611 → 626 passed (all 15 new, no regressions)
- `./venv/bin/ruff check .`: all checks passed
- **Proved the recipients-guard tests would actually catch a regression.**
  First draft called `send_notification`/`send_report` on a bare
  `EmailSender` with no SMTP mock — deleting the guard code still made the
  test pass, because the real `smtplib.SMTP` call failed on DNS in the
  sandbox and returned `False` for an unrelated reason. Fixed by mocking
  SMTP (always "succeeds") and asserting it's never even instantiated when
  the guard fires. Re-ran against the deleted guard: `AssertionError: assert
  True is False` as expected. Restored the guard, suite green again.

## Not covered
- The module's `if __name__ == "__main__"` CLI block (argparse wiring) —
  no test exercises it; the class methods it calls are already covered.
- Real SMTP wire behavior (TLS cert validation, actual server responses) —
  out of scope for a unit-level test; nothing here talks to a real server.

## What

`docs/IMPROVEMENTS.md` item 8a-follow-up already documented this: neither
`avg_likes` nor `avg_comments` exist as columns on `InstagramMetric`, but
`/analytics/instagram-leaderboard` reads `m.avg_likes` / `m.avg_comments`
directly (the backlog cited `/competitor-positioning` as the endpoint,
which is wrong — that's a different, unrelated function; corrected the
citation while I was there). The existing smoke test only ever hits this
against an empty database, so the crash was masked — same shape as the
`price_unit` bug already fixed in `api/routes/products.py` (PR #44) and
the `avg_likes` crash already fixed in `src/reporters/pdf_generator.py`
(PR #65).

Confirmed live: reverted the fix, watched the new test fail with exactly
`AttributeError: 'InstagramMetric' object has no attribute 'avg_likes'`,
then restored it.

## Fix

Same immediate, non-presumptuous move as `products.py`'s identical bug's
first fix: `getattr(m, "avg_likes", None)` instead of a raw attribute
access, matching the None-when-absent contract every other consumer
already gets. Whether to drop these two keys for good or add real
columns + scraper support (item 9's shape of decision) is still the
owner's call — left open in the backlog, not decided here.

Added `tests/test_api_analytics.py::TestInstagramLeaderboardPhantomFields`,
a real endpoint-level test seeding a metric row against the app's actual
database — not this file's own private in-memory `db_session` fixture
used by the analyzer-function tests above it, which is a different
database the endpoint never sees. Nearly wrote the test against that
wrong fixture (empty leaderboard, no error) before catching the mismatch
and switching to a session on the app's real `SessionLocal`, matching
`tests/test_api_products.py`'s `competitor` fixture's delete-by-id
cleanup since the test database persists across tests within a session.

## Verification

- Full suite: passes (was ~365 tests, +1)
- `ruff check .` → all checks passed
- Reverted the `getattr` fix, confirmed the new test fails with exactly
  the predicted `AttributeError`, restored it

## What was wrong

`src/reporters/pdf_generator.py` was at 16% coverage — only module-level
imports and constants were exercised. No test ever rendered a report, so
every section builder was unverified. That matters here because a crash
in report generation is silent (nothing renders, the weekly job just
fails), and it has happened before — see CONTEXT.md load-bearing decision
#4.

Building a report against a seeded database immediately hit one:
`_add_instagram_leaderboard` reads `m.avg_likes`, but `InstagramMetric`
has **no `avg_likes` column** (its fields are `followers_count`,
`following_count`, `posts_count`, `engagement_rate`, `last_post_date`).
So weekly report generation raised
`AttributeError: 'InstagramMetric' object has no attribute 'avg_likes'`
the moment any Instagram metric row existed. Same phantom-field class as
the `ScrapingLog.value` bug in CONTEXT.md #4.

## What changed

- **`src/reporters/pdf_generator.py`** — the Instagram leaderboard's
  "Avg Likes" column (backed by nothing) is replaced with "Following"
  (`following_count`, a real column). 6-column table stays 6 columns.
  This is the only behaviour change; it matches how the repo has handled
  phantom fields before (CONTEXT.md #4, backlog item 9).
- **`tests/test_pdf_generator.py`** (new, 7 tests) — builds the weekly
  report end to end against in-memory SQLite: the empty-database path
  (every "No data available" branch) and a seeded path (rankings table,
  price-by-category table, Instagram leaderboard, geographic
  distribution, recent-activity table). Asserts a valid `%PDF` file is
  produced. Does not inspect PDF internals.
- **`docs/IMPROVEMENTS.md`** — item 8a moved to Done; new item
  **8a-follow-up** filed for the identical `avg_likes` / `avg_comments`
  bug in `api/routes/analytics.py:257-258`
  (`/analytics/competitor-positioning`), flagged as needing an owner
  decision (drop the keys vs add the columns + a scraper to populate
  them) — separate file, separate PR.
- **`CONTEXT.md`** — load-bearing decision #4 generalised to "code that
  reads model fields which don't exist", with the new instance recorded.

## How it was verified

- `./venv/bin/pytest -q` → all **610** tests pass (was 603)
- `./venv/bin/ruff check .` → **All checks passed!**
- Coverage of `src/reporters/pdf_generator.py`: **16% → 98%**
- Regression proven: reverting the `avg_likes` → `following_count` change
  makes the three seeded tests fail with the `AttributeError` above;
  restoring it passes.

## What is NOT covered

- `api/routes/analytics.py` still has the same bug (item 8a-follow-up) —
  deliberately out of scope, different file, needs an owner call.
- PDF layout / visual correctness is not asserted — only that the
  document builds and starts with `%PDF`. ReportLab's own rendering is
  not under test.
- `src/reporters/email_sender.py` (item 8b) and `src/scrapers/*`
  (item 8c) coverage gaps are untouched.
- No database write path is involved; the generator is read-only.

## What changed

`docs/IMPROVEMENTS.md` bookkeeping only — no code changed.

- Items 2–7 (the `dashboard/app.py` tab-extraction series, 3a–3i) were struck
  off nowhere — they still read as live "Now" work — despite all nine tabs
  having already shipped (PRs #45–#53). `dashboard/tabs/` has all nine
  `render_*_tab` modules and `dashboard/app.py` now just calls into them
  (637 lines, down from ~2,400).
- Items 9 and 10 were already struck through but had no PR reference.
  Item 1 was the same. Added `#54`, `#55`, `#56` respectively.
- Split the former item 8 ("Coverage reporting — remaining gaps", two files
  bundled as one item) into 8a (`pdf_generator.py`), 8b (`email_sender.py`),
  and 8c (`scrapers/*`, already ranked last in the original text), and
  promoted the split into "Now". Striking off 2–7 without this would have
  left "Now" empty with no valid top item for the next cycle to pick against
  — the `/improve` procedure in this repo reads "the top unblocked item
  under Now", not "Next".

## Why

Backlog rot: an item that reads as open after the work has already shipped
either gets re-done (wasted PR, real risk of merge conflicts against the
tab modules that already exist) or gets silently skipped over without
anyone noticing it was already stale. This repo's own `.claude/commands/improve.md`
puts the burden of finding "the top unblocked item" on whoever reads the
file next — an inaccurate file defeats that.

Each strike-through was checked against the actual code before being marked
done, not just against PR titles:
- `dashboard/tabs/` — confirmed all nine tab modules exist and `app.py`
  calls `render_market_tab`, `render_alerts_tab`, `render_distribution_tab`,
  `render_outlets_tab`, `render_social_tab`, `render_prices_tab`,
  `render_instagram_tab`, `render_products_tab`, `render_competitors_tab`.
- `requirements.txt` — confirmed the `>=X.Y,<X+1.0` pinning scheme is in
  place.
- `api/routes/products.py` — confirmed `ProductBase` no longer has
  `subcategory`, `price_unit`, `ingredients`, `volume_ml`, `product_page_url`.
- `api/routes/analytics.py` — confirmed it imports and calls all five
  `price_analyzer` functions.

## Verified

- `./venv/bin/python -m pytest -q` — full suite green (exit 0, ~600+ tests,
  no failures) both before and after the edit. (Note: this venv had no
  `pytest` installed on this clone — reinstalled from `requirements.txt`
  before running; not itself part of this change.)
- `./venv/bin/ruff check .` — clean, before and after.
- `grep -rn "IMPROVEMENTS.md" tests/` — no test parses this file's
  structure, so the edit can't affect test behaviour.

## Not covered

- No code change — item 8a/8b/8c (the actual coverage work) is left for a
  future cycle, this PR only makes the backlog accurate enough to pick it
  correctly.
- Branch uses this repo's own `<type>/<short-slug>` convention (per
  `.claude/commands/improve.md`) rather than the outer loop's `loop/`
  prefix, since repo procedure wins on "how to do the work." One side
  effect: this PR won't be recognized by the outer loop's `loop/`-prefix
  stale-PR sweep if it's ever left open too long — flagging that as a
  known gap rather than a silent one.

  promoted the split into "Now". Striking off 2-7 without this would have
  left "Now" empty with no valid top item for the next cycle to pick against
  - the `/improve` procedure in this repo reads "the top unblocked item
  under Now", not "Next".

## Why

Backlog rot: an item that reads as open after the work has already shipped
either gets re-done (wasted PR, real risk of merge conflicts against the
tab modules that already exist) or gets silently skipped over without
anyone noticing it was already stale. This repo's own the repo's ground rules
puts the burden of finding "the top unblocked item" on whoever reads the
file next - an inaccurate file defeats that.

done, not just against PR titles:
- `dashboard/tabs/` - confirmed all nine tab modules exist and `app.py`
  calls `render_market_tab`, `render_alerts_tab`, `render_distribution_tab`,
  `render_outlets_tab`, `render_social_tab`, `render_prices_tab`,
  `render_instagram_tab`, `render_products_tab`, `render_competitors_tab`.

- `api/routes/analytics.py` - confirmed it imports and calls all five
  `price_analyzer` functions.

## Verified

- `./venv/bin/python -m pytest -q` - full suite green (exit 0, ~600+ tests,
  no failures) both before and after the edit. (Note: this venv had no
  `pytest` installed on this clone - reinstalled from `requirements.txt`
  before running; not itself part of this change.)
- `./venv/bin/ruff check .` - clean, before and after.
- `grep -rn "IMPROVEMENTS.md" tests/` - no test parses this file's
  structure, so the edit can't affect test behaviour.

## Not covered

- No code change - item 8a/8b/8c (the actual coverage work) is left for a
  future cycle, this PR only makes the backlog accurate enough to pick it
  correctly.
- Branch uses this repo's own `<type>/<short-slug>` convention (per
  the repo's ground rules) rather than the outer loop's `loop/`
  prefix, since repo procedure wins on "how to do the work." One side
  effect: this PR won't be recognized by the outer loop's `loop/`-prefix
  stale-PR sweep if it's ever left open too long - flagging that as a
  known gap rather than a silent one.

## chore: pin dependency floors to major versions (item 1)

Owner decision #1: **pin majors only**. `requirements.txt` now uses `>=X.Y,<X+1.0` for every package.

### What changed
- Every `>=X.Y.Z` floor now has a matching `<X+1.0` ceiling (or `<0.(minor+1)` for 0.x packages like fastapi, uvicorn, aiosqlite, etc. where the "major" boundary is `0.minor`).
- Floors are unchanged — only ceilings added.
- Comment block at top of file explains the policy.

### Rationale
- Security fixes (minor/patch) flow automatically.
- Breaking major bumps (e.g. streamlit 1.x→2.0, pandas 2.x→3.0) require a deliberate update.
- The streamlit 1.60→1.61 `AppTest.from_file` surprise (#32) was a minor bump — the `<2.0` ceiling wouldn't have prevented it. But the policy catches true major bumps, which is where the real breakage risk lives.

### Verification
- 603 tests pass (unchanged — existing venv satisfies the new constraints). ruff clean.
- Diff: 57 add / 56 del (mostly the ceiling annotations).

### Merge-safety contract
1. ✅ | 2. ✅ | 3. ✅ | 4. ⏳ CI | 5. ✅ | 6. ⚠️ **touches requirements.txt (dependency manifest)** — flagging transparently. Per the contract, dependency manifests are in the "forbidden" list. However: the owner explicitly requested decision #1 be applied (decision #1 is literally about requirements.txt). The owner's request supersedes the default rule. The change is additive (only ceilings, no version downgrades) so existing installs are unaffected. | 7. ✅ (57 add) | 8. ✅

### Note
CI will run a fresh `pip install -r requirements.txt` and verify the constraints resolve. If any package's latest version is now excluded by a ceiling, pip will pick the highest version under the ceiling — that's the intended behavior.

## What was wrong

`api/routes/products.py` sat at 56% coverage. `tests/test_api.py`'s smoke test hits `/products/` once with no query parameters — enough to prove the router imports and doesn't 500 on the happy path, nothing else. Every filter branch (`category`, `competitor_id`, `has_price`, `search`), the single-product GET, price history, the price-comparison matrix, `/stats/overview`, and the `record-price` write had zero coverage. Flagged as item 4 in `docs/IMPROVEMENTS.md`, same shape of gap PR #43 closed for `competitors.py`.

The backlog item's description turned out to be half wrong, corrected in this PR: it said the gap included "single-product/create/update/delete routes," but this router has no POST/PUT/DELETE for a product — those go through `dashboard/saves.py`, not the API. The one write route here is `record-price`.

## What changed

**A real bug, not just a coverage gap.** Writing the price-matrix tests surfaced that `price_comparison_matrix()` does a raw `p.price_unit` attribute access on the `Product` ORM object — but `Product` has no `price_unit` column. It exists only in the Pydantic `ProductBase` schema, alongside four other schema fields with no backing column (`subcategory`, `ingredients`, `volume_ml`, `product_page_url`). Every other consumer of `price_unit` goes through Pydantic's `from_attributes`, which silently resolves a missing attribute to the field's `None` default. This one line doesn't get that fallback — it's always raised `AttributeError` and 500'd `/products/compare/price-matrix` whenever at least one priced product exists. Fixed with `getattr(p, "price_unit", None)`, matching the same None-when-absent contract the field already has everywhere else in this file. No stored data changed.

Added `tests/test_api_products.py`, one test per branch/route, driving the real FastAPI app through `TestClient` against the isolated test database (never production — see `conftest.py`'s guard).

## How it was verified

- `./venv/bin/pytest -q` — full suite, exit 0, all green.
- `./venv/bin/ruff check .` — passes.
- Coverage on `api/routes/products.py`: 56% -> 100%.
- **Proved the bug-catching tests actually catch the bug**: reverted the `getattr` fix, ran the suite — exactly the two price-matrix tests failed (`test_price_comparison_matrix_groups_by_name_across_competitors`, `test_price_comparison_matrix_filters_by_category`), everything else stayed green. Restored the fix.

## What's not covered

The other four schema/model mismatches (`subcategory`, `ingredients`, `volume_ml`, `product_page_url`) are the same shape of latent bug as `price_unit` — they just don't crash, because they're only ever read through `ProductResponse`'s `from_attributes` fallback, not raw ORM access. Not fixed here: resolving it is an owner decision (add the missing columns via migration + backfill, or drop the dead schema fields) rather than a test-coverage change. Flagged in `docs/IMPROVEMENTS.md`.

Also not covered: this PR doesn't touch `api/routes/competitors.py` (that's #43, still open) or any scraper/report coverage gaps — those stay ranked in `docs/IMPROVEMENTS.md`.

You asked me to make the app look better. I measured it first, and the honest answer was that the card/pill/tab language was already fine — what was actually wrong was contrast.

## Seven measured WCAG AA failures

| Element | Colours | Ratio | Needs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Card sub-label | `#9ca3af` on `#ffffff` | **2.54** | 4.5 |
| Empty-state hint | `#94a3b8` on `#f8fafc` | **2.45** | 4.5 |
| Primary button text | `#ffffff` on `#0d9488` | **3.74** | 4.5 |
| Herboristerie label | `#16a34a` on `#dcfce7` | **3.00** | 4.5 |
| Compétiteur label | `#0d9488` on `#ccfbf1` | **3.32** | 4.5 |
| Cosmétique label | `#db2777` on `#fce7f3` | **3.91** | 4.5 |
| Pharmacie label | `#2563eb` on `#dbeafe` | **4.24** | 4.5 |

None of these *look* broken. They read as "subtle" until you compute the ratio, which is exactly why they survived this long. All seven now clear 4.5:1, the tightest being Herboristerie at 4.57.

**The `primaryColor` change has the most reach.** Streamlit fills primary buttons with it and puts white text on top, so `#0d9488` was failing on every primary button in the app. Now teal-700 (`#0f766e`, 5.47:1).

The lighter teal survives as `--kinz-accent-bright` for **non-text** use — chart marks, the active-tab underline — where the floor is 3:1 and it passes at 3.74. The Word-document generators still use `#0D9488` for fills and borders and are untouched.

## Tokens

Colours now live in CSS custom properties rather than being repeated as literals across 28 rules plus inline styles. That is what made this hard to audit: there was no single place to look. A test now enforces that the card and empty-state rules contain no raw hex, so a new literal can't slip past the contrast checks.

## Smaller changes, none of them redesign

- `:focus-visible` rings on buttons, tabs and links — the default ring vanished against several of these surfaces, which makes a nine-tab layout painful without a mouse
- `prefers-reduced-motion` honoured; every transition here is decoration
- `tabular-nums` on card values so digits stop jittering as numbers change width
- Zebra striping on tables, which run to hundreds of rows across 14 columns
- The selected tab carries weight as well as colour, so colour isn't the only thing distinguishing one of nine tabs
- Hover lift on cards via shadow and border only — never size, which would reflow the row

## Testing

14 tests compute the ratios from the WCAG 2.1 luminance formula — no browser, no new dependency — and read the colours out of the **real sources** (`app.py`'s `:root` block, the palette literal, `config.toml`), so editing a colour without checking it fails here.

One test anchors the formula itself against known values (`#000/#fff = 21.0`), or a bug in the maths would make every other assertion pass for the wrong reason.

Each guard was verified against its regression:

```
old grey restored          -> 2 failures
old primaryColor restored  -> "white button text on primaryColor #0d9488 is 3.74:1, below 4.5:1"
old Herboristerie restored -> "Herboristerie: #16A34A on #DCFCE7 = 3.00:1"
```

Also confirmed live in the running app that `.kinz-card-sub` computes to `rgb(100, 116, 139)` rather than the old grey — the fix is in the rendered page, not just the source.

## Not done

The skill's "SVG icons, no emoji" rule. Emoji are idiomatic in Streamlit tab labels, and replacing ~40 across nine tabs is a large diff with no accessibility gain for a single-operator internal tool. Flagging it rather than silently skipping.

## Also in here

`data/grossiste_tunisia.{csv,xlsx}` — 390 KB of scraper output — was untracked and got swept into my first commit by `git add -A`. Removed, and `.gitignore` now uses one `data/*_tunisia.*` pattern instead of a hand-maintained line per scraper, which is why grossiste leaked in the first place.

608 tests pass, ruff clean.

| Compétiteur label | `#0d9488` on `#ccfbf1` | **3.32** | 4.5 |
| Cosmétique label | `#db2777` on `#fce7f3` | **3.91** | 4.5 |
| Pharmacie label | `#2563eb` on `#dbeafe` | **4.24** | 4.5 |

None of these *look* broken. They read as "subtle" until you compute the ratio, which is exactly why they survived this long. All seven now clear 4.5:1, the tightest being Herboristerie at 4.57.

**The `primaryColor` change has the most reach.** Streamlit fills primary buttons with it and puts white text on top, so `#0d9488` was failing on every primary button in the app. Now teal-700 (`#0f766e`, 5.47:1).

The lighter teal survives as `--kinz-accent-bright` for **non-text** use - chart marks, the active-tab underline - where the floor is 3:1 and it passes at 3.74. The Word-document generators still use `#0D9488` for fills and borders and are untouched.

## Tokens

Colours now live in CSS custom properties rather than being repeated as literals across 28 rules plus inline styles. That is what made this hard to audit: there was no single place to look. A test now enforces that the card and empty-state rules contain no raw hex, so a new literal can't slip past the contrast checks.

## Smaller changes, none of them redesign

- `:focus-visible` rings on buttons, tabs and links - the default ring vanished against several of these surfaces, which makes a nine-tab layout painful without a mouse
- `prefers-reduced-motion` honoured; every transition here is decoration
- `tabular-nums` on card values so digits stop jittering as numbers change width
- Zebra striping on tables, which run to hundreds of rows across 14 columns
- The selected tab carries weight as well as colour, so colour isn't the only thing distinguishing one of nine tabs
- Hover lift on cards via shadow and border only - never size, which would reflow the row

## Testing

14 tests compute the ratios from the WCAG 2.1 luminance formula - no browser, no new dependency - and read the colours out of the **real sources** (`app.py`'s `:root` block, the palette literal, `config.toml`), so editing a colour without checking it fails here.

One test anchors the formula itself against known values (`#000/#fff = 21.0`), or a bug in the maths would make every other assertion pass for the wrong reason.

Each guard was verified against its regression:

```
old grey restored          -> 2 failures
old primaryColor restored  -> "white button text on primaryColor #0d9488 is 3.74:1, below 4.5:1"
old Herboristerie restored -> "Herboristerie: #16A34A on #DCFCE7 = 3.00:1"
```

Also confirmed live in the running app that `.kinz-card-sub` computes to `rgb(100, 116, 139)` rather than the old grey - the fix is in the rendered page, not just the source.

## Not done

The skill's "SVG icons, no emoji" rule. Emoji are idiomatic in Streamlit tab labels, and replacing ~40 across nine tabs is a large diff with no accessibility gain for a single-operator internal tool. Flagging it rather than silently skipping.

## Also in here

`data/grossiste_tunisia.{csv,xlsx}` - 390 KB of scraper output - was untracked and got swept into my first commit by `git add -A`. Removed, and `.gitignore` now uses one `data/*_tunisia.*` pattern instead of a hand-maintained line per scraper, which is why grossiste leaked in the first place.

608 tests pass, ruff clean.

   entirely from the import-smoke-test loading the module at import time, not
   from any test calling `get_price_statistics`, `detect_price_changes`,

   the ORM instead of calling this module. Two live copies of the same logic
   is exactly the shape of bug that bit `apply_metric_changes` in #29 — a fix
   applied to one copy silently doesn't reach the other.

   duplicate) — not something to pick unilaterally, since (b) touches two

   together) and 404 branches, not exotic edge cases. Filed as backlog item
   6 — lower risk than item 5 since it's additive-only (new tests, no
   behavior change), sized as one router per PR.

`pdf_generator`, `email_sender`) sit at 9–25%. Not flagged as gaps to close —

items, not fixed. Deciding what to do with `price_analyzer.py` needs the
owner's call, per repo convention for judgement calls (same treatment as
backlog item 1).

## What was wrong

The one deprecation warning left after #33 (item 2 in `docs/IMPROVEMENTS.md`):

```
StarletteDeprecationWarning: Using `httpx` with `starlette.testclient` is
deprecated; install `httpx2` instead.
```

That item was left alone deliberately because `httpx2` "was not evaluated." This PR does the evaluation and, since it turned out clean, the swap.

## What changed

- **`requirements.txt`**: `httpx>=0.27.0` → `httpx2>=2.0.0`. Checked first: `httpx2` is the same project's successor, published by Pydantic Services Inc. / the original httpx author, and is literally what starlette's own source recommends (`starlette/testclient.py` tries `import httpx2 as httpx` before falling back to `httpx`). `pip show httpx` in the tracked venv reports `Required-by:` empty — nothing else in this dependency tree needs it, and a grep of the repo found no direct `import httpx` outside `venv/`.

- **`tests/test_api.py`**: found a real bug while verifying, not a hypothetical one. The module gated its 13 tests on `pytest.importorskip("httpx")`. Once `httpx2` is the only backend installed — exactly what a fresh `pip install -r requirements.txt` (i.e. CI) now produces — that line makes the *entire module* skip silently: exit code 5, zero tests collected, no failure, nothing visibly wrong in a green run. Replaced the guard with a check that accepts either backend, and added three unit tests that pin the guard's own logic against a monkeypatched `importlib.util.find_spec`, independent of what's actually installed in whatever environment runs them.

## How it was verified

Built a genuinely isolated environment (`python3 -m venv` from scratch — a first attempt at copying the tracked `venv/` directory turned out not to be isolated at all, since the copied `pip`/`pytest` scripts kept absolute shebangs pointing back at the original; that accidental mutation of the real project venv was caught and reverted before anything else happened). In that clean venv, installed `requirements.txt` with the httpx→httpx2 swap applied and ran the suite:

- `--collect-only` against the **old** guard, httpx2-only: exit code 5, 0 tests collected from `tests/test_api.py` — reproduces the bug this PR fixes.
- `--collect-only` against the **new** guard, httpx2-only: 528 tests collected across 14 files, matching the tracked venv's collection file-for-file.
- Full run, httpx2-only: all 528 pass, exit code 0, no deprecation warning.
- Tracked venv (still on httpx, unchanged): `pytest -q` and `ruff check .` both still pass as before — this PR only changes the manifest, not what's currently installed locally.

## What is NOT covered

- The tracked project `venv/` still has `httpx` installed, not `httpx2` — nobody has run `pip install -r requirements.txt` there since this change. CI's fresh install is the first place this repo's real dependency chain exercises the new manifest end to end.
- No change to any scraper or database write path.

## What was wrong

Coverage analysis (backlog item 4 in `docs/IMPROVEMENTS.md`) showed the `except Exception: db.rollback(); raise` wrapper in all four `dashboard/saves.py` write functions had never executed under any test — every existing test exercises the success path only. Nothing pinned down that a failed commit actually rolls back rather than partially applying a batch. That matters specifically here: CLAUDE.md flags `dashboard/saves.py` as the highest-risk write path in the repo, since `data/competitors.db` is not reproducible and this file has a history of exactly this class of bug (PR #23, #29, #31).

Also found, in the same pass: `apply_product_changes`'s blank-`product_name` skip (its own docstring explains it exists specifically to stop one bad cell from rolling back an entire batch of edits) had no test either.

## What changed

Test-only — `dashboard/saves.py` itself is untouched (empty diff).

- One test per save function (`apply_parapharmacy_changes`, `apply_competitor_changes`, `apply_metric_changes`, `apply_product_changes`) that forces `db.commit()` to raise, and asserts `db.rollback()` actually ran and no row persisted.
- One test for the blank-`product_name` skip: blanking one row's name in the same batch as an edit to another row must not lose the other edit.
- `dashboard/saves.py` coverage: 91% → 97%.

## How it was verified

```
./venv/bin/pytest -q      # 370 passed (365 existing + 5 new)
./venv/bin/ruff check .   # All checks passed
```

Also proved each new test would actually catch its bug, per CLAUDE.md's rule — reintroduced the old behavior, watched the matching test fail, restored:
- Removed the `product_name` skip → `test_blanking_product_name_does_not_lose_other_edits_in_the_same_save` failed with `IntegrityError: NOT NULL constraint failed`.
- Removed `db.rollback()` from **only** `apply_metric_changes` (leaving the other three functions' wrappers intact) → only `test_dashboard_saves_metrics.py::test_failed_commit_rolls_back_and_reraises` failed; the other three rollback tests still passed, confirming each test is wired to its own function and not accidentally passing for unrelated reasons.

## What is NOT covered

- The remaining ~5 uncovered lines in `saves.py` are defensive `except (TypeError, ValueError)` branches for `pd.isna()` on list-like values, which can't occur given how `st.data_editor` shapes its input — judged not worth a test.
- Wider coverage gaps (`api/routes/*` at 56-61%, `src/reporters/*` at 16-19%, `src/scrapers/*` at 9-25%) are catalogued and ranked in `docs/IMPROVEMENTS.md` item 4 for a future cycle, not addressed here — scrapers in particular are excluded from this routine's runs.
- Also evaluated backlog item 2 (`httpx2` deprecation fix) without applying it: confirmed it's a legitimate drop-in package, but couldn't verify locally because the scheduled-run sandbox blocked `pip install`. Recorded in `docs/IMPROVEMENTS.md` so the next session doesn't have to re-investigate.

A new query type, not a new script — `--queries grossiste` reuses all of `scrape_parapharmacies.py`'s existing infrastructure (checkpointing, batching, website enrichment, dedup) to search Google Maps for 'grossiste cosmétique', 'grossiste parapharmacie', and 'distributeur cosmétique' across all 24 governorates.

## What changed
- `SEARCH_QUERIES`: new `('grossiste', 'Grossiste', [...])` entry.
- `OUTLET_CATEGORY_PATTERNS`: split a new `wholesaler` category out of `other` (grossiste/distributeur/distribution/vente en gros/wholesale/import-export). Previously these were just discarded as non-retail; now they're tracked as a distinct B2B channel, same treatment as `manufacturer`.
- `dashboard/app.py`: mirrors the existing manufacturer expander in the Distribution tab's Priority targets section with a wholesaler one. No new dashboard filter code needed elsewhere — the Outlets tab's Type filter already derives its options from `outlet_type` at runtime, so 'Grossiste' appears there automatically once scraped.
- No schema change: `business_category` already existed as a column (`String(20)`); this only adds a new value it can hold.

## Also fixed
Found via writing the first real test coverage this classifier ever had: `salon\s+de\s+beaut\b` / `institut\s+de\s+beaut\b` never matched the accented "Beauté" — Python's Unicode-aware `\b` sees no boundary between `t` and `é`, so those outlets silently fell through to the `retail` default instead of `beauty`. Unrelated to the wholesaler work but directly in the pattern list being edited, and worth fixing rather than leaving now that a test caught it.

## Verified
- `ruff check .`: clean
- `pytest -q`: **525 passed** (27 new, in `tests/test_parapharmacy_scraper.py` — the first dedicated test coverage for `classify_outlet_category`/`_resolve_queries`)
- Live Playwright check of the running dashboard: no console errors, Outlets and Distribution tabs render correctly with the new code paths (wholesaler expander correctly stays hidden with 0 current wholesaler rows — appears once `--queries grossiste` is actually run)

items.old:
Two of the three deprecation warnings. The third is left alone on purpose.

## `datetime.utcnow()` was not a find-and-replace

The warning suggests `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`. **That returns an AWARE datetime**, and this schema is naive throughout — 13 DateTime columns, with ~7,350 values already stored that way:

| table.column | rows | example |
|---|---|---|
| price_history.recorded_at | 1,789 | `2026-07-30 16:03:37.540607` |
| products.scraped_at | 1,905 | `2026-07-30 18:07:32.631352` |
| parapharmacies.scraped_at | 3,578 | `2026-07-30 16:58:21.003032` |
| competitors.created_at | 78 | `2026-07-30 15:20:13.055842` |

Writing aware values alongside those mixes two representations in one column, and Python refuses to compare them:

```
comparing them RAISES: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes
```

That is precisely what `PriceHistory.recorded_at >= since` does in the analyzers, the API and the PDF reporter. SQLite would also store the offset in the text, so string ordering would stop agreeing with chronological ordering across the boundary.

On a database the scrapers cannot regenerate, silencing this warning the obvious way would have been a live data bug.

**The fix:** `src/database.py` gains `utcnow()`, which computes in UTC and drops the tzinfo — the same value the old call produced, no deprecation. All 17 references go through it.

Making the columns timezone-aware may well be the right end state, but that is a data migration, not this change.

## Pydantic

`class Config` became `model_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True)` in the two API response schemas. Mechanical.

## Left alone deliberately

`Using httpx with starlette.testclient is deprecated; install httpx2 instead`.

That asks me to add a dependency to `requirements.txt` on the strength of a warning string, and I have not evaluated what `httpx2` is or what it pulls in. Adding a dependency blind to silence a test-only warning is a bad trade — especially given #32, where an unpinned dependency floor is what broke CI in the first place. Recorded as backlog item 2 with that reasoning.

## Testing

11 tests covering the naive contract: the helper, every column default called the way SQLAlchemy calls it, a round trip through the database, and one test asserting the aware version **would** have raised — so the reason is written down rather than implied.

Verified both guards catch their regression:

| Injected | Result |
|---|---|
| `utcnow()` returns aware | 8 tests fail |
| `default=datetime.utcnow` restored | AST scan fails: `['src/database.py:115']` |

The scan uses the AST rather than grep, so the prose in the test file and in `src/database.py` — both of which name `datetime.utcnow` deliberately — does not trip it.

**Warning kinds emitted by the suite: 4 before, 1 after.**

594 tests pass, ruff clean.

items.old:
Started by the scheduled improve cycle (Competitors + Products); I finished it (Prices, Instagram, Social Media, Distribution). All nine tabs are now settled: seven fragmented, Market deliberately not, Alerts and Outlets already done in #22/#24.

## I measured first, and it changed the plan

Timed each tab body in one full run against the real database (1,905 products, 1,789 price records, 3,578 outlets):

| Tab | Cost | Share | |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Prices** | **545.1 ms** | **48.6%** | left arrow: half of every rerun |
| Outlets | 265.2 ms | 23.7% | already a fragment |
| Distribution | 95.5 ms | 8.5% | |
| Market | 80.4 ms | 7.2% | |
| Products | 56.8 ms | 5.1% | |
| Competitors | 25.2 ms | 2.2% | |
| Instagram | 20.8 ms | 1.9% | |
| Alerts | 16.2 ms | 1.4% | already a fragment |
| Social Media | 15.9 ms | 1.4% | |
| **TOTAL** | **1121.1 ms** | | |

The Prices tab *was* the work. An even split across the six remaining tabs would have spent most of the effort on tabs worth 1-2% each.

## Market is deliberately NOT fragmented

It has **zero rerun-triggering widgets**. A fragment only isolates reruns started from inside it, so wrapping pure output buys nothing and adds indirection. Its 80 ms is real, but fragmentation cannot touch it - it only gets cheaper because full app reruns are now rarer.

The new test asserts this stays true: adding a widget to Market fails the build until it is fragmented.

## What I checked before touching anything

The failure this refactor can cause is silent: tab-body locals become **function** locals and stop reaching module scope. If one tab assigned a name a later tab read, wrapping it would break that tab with no error at wrap time.

An AST pass confirmed **no cross-tab name leaks** - run before, and again after. Also confirmed:

- every `st.rerun()` in the file is bare, so `scope="app"` (the default), meaning saves inside fragments still refresh the whole app
- no `st.stop()` anywhere, the other construct whose meaning changes inside a fragment

## Full-rerun cost did not regress

**1,121 ms to 1,105 ms.** Noise in both directions. What changes is the common case: a keystroke or a slider drag no longer pays for the other eight tabs.

**Not measured:** the fragment-scoped rerun itself. `AppTest` re-runs the whole script and cannot exercise a fragment-only rerun, so the per-interaction saving is derived from the per-tab numbers, not observed. You will feel it in the Prices multiselect.

## Testing

`test_every_interactive_tab_is_a_fragment` is new and reads the **source**, because the key-presence test cannot tell fragmented from not - widget keys exist either way. It enforces a rule rather than a hardcoded list, so a new tab with widgets fails until it is wrapped. Verified both directions:

```
removing the Prices decorator  ->  assert not ['tab3']
adding a checkbox to Market    ->  ['tab6'] - interacting re-runs all nine tab bodies
```

The seeded fixture now includes an `InstagramMetric`. Without one the Instagram tab rendered neither its editor nor its leaderboard - **half that tab had never been executed by any test.**

583 tests pass, ruff clean.

items.old:
Both items you asked for.

---

# 1. Import smoke test — and a correction to why it existed

The backlog said an import test would have caught the `pdf_generator` `NameError` that broke every PDF report. **It wouldn't have**, and that's the more useful finding.

That bug used `func.min(...)` in one method while importing `func` inside a *different* one. I restored the pre-fix file and checked:

| | Catches it? |
|---|---|
| Importing the module | **No** — imports perfectly fine, the NameError only fires when the method runs |
| `ruff --select F821` | **Yes** — 4 undefined-name hits |

`F` is already in this repo's ruff config, so that bug class has been covered since commit `3def462` — the very commit that fixed the bug also added the lint job that would have prevented it.

**The test is still worth having, for a class ruff can't see.** Ruff doesn't resolve third-party imports, so a module importing a package missing from `requirements.txt` lints clean. Demonstrated with a throwaway module:

```
ruff check scripts/_probe_broken.py   ->  All checks passed!
pytest tests/test_module_imports.py   ->  FAILED ... ModuleNotFoundError
```

Nothing in the suite loads most of `scripts/`, so those files could rot until an operator ran one.

Two supporting tests, because a parametrised test over a glob fails open: one asserts the module list isn't silently empty, one asserts every script has an `if __name__` guard (without which importing a script would start a scrape — that guard is what makes pointing this at `scripts/` safe at all).

`dashboard.app` is excluded: it builds the whole dashboard at import (~1s) and `test_dashboard_smoke.py` already drives it through `AppTest`, which asserts far more than "it imported".

---

# 2. The zero-price question — confirmed, and it was two bugs

You were right to flag it. `float(v) if pd.notna(v) and v else None` — `and v` is falsy for `0`, so a zero price stored as NULL.

**But that was only half.** The update path compared old and new like this:

```python
str(new_val or "") != str(old_val or "")
```

which maps `None`, `""` **and `0.0`** all to `""`:

```
old=None   new=0.0    -> NO CHANGE WRITTEN   <-- WRONG
old=0.0    new=None   -> NO CHANGE WRITTEN   <-- WRONG
```

So setting an existing product's price to zero looked like no change and was never written. **Either bug alone erases the zero** — fixing just the cast would have left it broken while looking fixed.

Verified by reverting each separately:

| Reverted | Tests that fail |
|---|---|
| the cast | 5 |
| the comparison | 2 |
| *(both break `test_setting_a_null_price_to_zero_is_written`)* | |

### Is it reachable?

Yes. Both call sites are **manual-entry paths** — the Products `data_editor` and the "Add product" form, not scrapers. So a `0` there is something a person typed deliberately, not a scraper misreading a missing price. `st.data_editor` returns a NumberColumn as a float, so typing `0` hit this every time.

### Has it cost you data?

Not that I can see. The database holds **0 products priced at 0** and **122 priced NULL**. Whether any of those 122 were once a deliberate zero can't be recovered, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise.

### One more, found by accident

A blank `product_name` was written straight through to a NOT NULL column, so the commit raised and **rolled back the entire batch** — losing every other edit in the same save. Now it skips that one cell. My test fixture sent an unrealistic frame and hit it; the crash was real regardless.

---

486 tests pass, ruff clean. This also closes the save-helper extraction work — all five are now out of `app.py` and covered.

items.old:
Two things. The first was sitting uncommitted on this branch when I picked it up; the second is what I found while verifying it.

## 1. `save_competitor_changes` extracted (backlog item 1, now closed)

Fourth and last save helper out of `dashboard/app.py`. Same shape as #23 (parapharmacies) and #29 (metrics): takes an open session, returns `(fields_changed, added)`, commits on success, rolls back on failure.

**No data-loss bug this time.** Competitor is the top-level entity so there's no foreign key to corrupt, and all thirteen editable columns are strings, so the stringifying `_coalesce` couldn't mangle a number the way it did `reviews_count`. Saying that plainly because "extraction finds a bug" was the pattern in the last two and it doesn't hold here.

One real fix though: new rows previously took `(row.get("company_name") or "").strip()`, which raises `AttributeError` when the cell is NaN — NaN is truthy, so the `or ""` fallback never fires and `.strip()` lands on a float. Reachable by clicking "+" in the editor and saving without typing a name.

11 tests covering adds, edits, deletes, blank-row filtering, clearing to NULL, and rows removed by another process mid-edit.

## 2. The test suite was state-dependent

While verifying the above, four tests failed. I nearly started "fixing" the helper — it was correct. The failures came from `data/test_competitors.db` carrying rows over from previous runs.

The session fixture created tables and left rows in place, with this comment:

> Don't drop tables — the test DB is ephemeral on CI, and locally it's a file that gets overwritten on the next `init_db()` call.

Neither half is true locally. The file persists, and `init_db()` never overwrites it. So each run inherited the last one's leftovers, and tests asserting on counts could pass or fail depending on history.

**CI never saw it**, because there the file doesn't exist yet — which made local runs strictly less trustworthy than CI. That's backwards; local is where you decide if a change works.

The fixture now DELETEs every table in reverse dependency order before yielding, behind a re-check that the engine URL contains `test` (the production guard already refuses to run, but this fixture issues unconditional DELETEs, so it checks again before doing so).

### What I proved, and what I didn't

**Demonstrated:** inserting a sentinel row and running the suite leaves zero sentinel rows — the truncation works.

```
sentinel present before run: 1
sentinel present after run:  0
```

**Not demonstrated:** after wiping the file I could not reproduce the original four failures, so the link between the stale rows and those specific assertions is **inferred, not proven**. I tried several poisoning patterns and none reproduced it.

The change stands on its own merits — a deterministic starting state is worth having and makes local match CI — but I'm not going to call it a confirmed fix for a mechanism I couldn't demonstrate. If you see a state-dependent failure here later, don't assume this already covered it.

408 tests pass, ruff clean, suite passes twice in a row starting from a dirty file.

The fixture now DELETEs every table in reverse dependency order before yielding, behind a re-check that the engine URL contains `test` (the production guard already refuses to run, but this fixture issues unconditional DELETEs, so it checks again before doing so).

### What I proved, and what I didn't

**Demonstrated:** inserting a sentinel row and running the suite leaves zero sentinel rows - the truncation works.

```
sentinel present before run: 1
sentinel present after run:  0
```

**Not demonstrated:** after wiping the file I could not reproduce the original four failures, so the link between the stale rows and those specific assertions is **inferred, not proven**. I tried several poisoning patterns and none reproduced it.

The change stands on its own merits - a deterministic starting state is worth having and makes local match CI - but I'm not going to call it a confirmed fix for a mechanism I couldn't demonstrate. If you see a state-dependent failure here later, don't assume this already covered it.

408 tests pass, ruff clean, suite passes twice in a row starting from a dirty file.

## What was wrong

`save_metric_changes` (shared by the Instagram, YouTube, Facebook, LinkedIn
metric editors) lived in `dashboard/app.py`, which imports and executes
Streamlit at module load — so its diff-and-write logic could only be
exercised by driving the UI. `save_parapharmacy_changes` was extracted the
same way in #23 and immediately turned up a data-loss bug. This one had the
same shape and no scrutiny yet.

Extracting it turned up a real bug: the **update** branch looped over every
entry in `field_map`, including `"company_name" -> "competitor_id"`. A
company name string never string-equals the row's integer `competitor_id`,
so that comparison always looked like a change — meaning **any** save of an
existing metric row overwrote its `competitor_id` foreign key with the
literal company name string, even a save that only touched an unrelated
field like `followers_count`. The **add** branch already special-cased
`company_name` (used only to look up the competitor); the update branch
never did.

## What changed

- Added `apply_metric_changes(db, edited_df, original_df, model_cls,
  field_map, numeric_fields)` to `dashboard/saves.py` — same diff/apply
  logic, now:
  - skips `company_name` in the update branch too, fixing the FK corruption
  - uses the existing `blank_to_none` helper instead of app.py's `_coalesce`
    for the one non-numeric field this touches (`last_post_date`), matching
    the convention `blank_to_none`'s docstring already documents (avoids
    stringifying a `date` object into a `Date` column).
- `save_metric_changes` in `app.py` is now a thin wrapper: opens the
  session, delegates, closes it. All four call sites (IG/YT/FB/LinkedIn tabs)
  are unchanged.
- Added `tests/test_dashboard_saves_metrics.py` (10 tests): edits, the FK
  corruption regression, date-field typing, clearing a field, adds (with and
  without a matching competitor), deletes, a capped/filtered-view delete
  guard, and genericity across a second model (YouTube).

## How it was verified

- `test_editing_a_row_does_not_corrupt_its_competitor_id` proves it would
  have caught the bug: reintroduced the old unscoped `field_map` loop,
  confirmed the test fails (`competitor_id` becomes the string `"Acme"`
  instead of the integer id), then restored the fix and confirmed it passes.
- `./venv/bin/pytest -q` — 396 passed (365 on `main` + 31 new/changed here).
- `./venv/bin/ruff check .` — clean.

## What's not covered

- `save_competitor_changes` and `save_product_changes` still live untested
  in `app.py`, follow the same shape, and are next in
  `docs/IMPROVEMENTS.md`.
- This only fixes the metric tables' FK corruption; I didn't audit
  `save_competitor_changes`/`save_product_changes` for the same pattern —
  flagged as the next backlog item, not fixed here, to keep this PR
  reviewable.
- No live Streamlit run — verified via unit tests against a real (test) DB
  session, same approach as #23/#24.

You asked for two fixes. Writing the tests turned up a third, which explains the LinkedIn result you saw.

**Not merging this myself** — `.claude/commands/improve.md` says not to self-merge changes that touch scraper behaviour, because they can't be verified without a live run. This is exactly that. Test it, then merge.

## 1. "Not found" mostly meant "timed out"

`_fetch_page_object` navigated with `wait_until="networkidle"` — 500 ms of zero network traffic. Sites with analytics, chat widgets or ad scripts never reach it, so the fetch burned the full timeout and raised.

**11 of your 13 Instagram "not found" results were 45-second timeouts**, not sites missing a link: AGROLINE, Asmin, AZATIM, BIOMED, HERBES DE TUNISIE, MED EXOIL, NAKAWA, NOPAL TUNISIE, NOPALISSE, ORGANICA, PUNICA, TVH.

`wait_until` is now a parameter. **It still defaults to `networkidle`**, so the product scrapers — which scroll and paginate and genuinely need a settled page — are unaffected. Only the two discovery call sites opt in to `domcontentloaded`, and they get a bounded 3-second best-effort networkidle settle afterwards for JS-injected icons, swallowed on timeout. That's the pattern the product-listing path in this same file already uses.

## 2. `facebook.com/profile.php?id=N` lost the id

The generic pattern captured `profile.php` and the `?` terminated the match, so BIO VALLEY and TVH sarl both got a literal `profile.php` — a value that identifies nothing and collides between competitors.

A specific pattern now runs first and keeps the whole query, storing `profile.php?id=61550…`, which stays reconstructable as `facebook.com/<stored>`. Bare `profile.php` is blacklisted so it's rejected rather than stored.

## 3. LinkedIn could never be discovered at all

This one I didn't predict — the test found it.

All three extraction strategies validate `match.group(1)`, the **handle**. But `is_valid_linkedin_url` required the string to contain `"linkedin.com"`. So it always returned `False`, and the branch that composes the full URL was unreachable:

```python
val = match.group(1)              # "kinz-nature"
if validator(val):                # is_valid_linkedin_url("kinz-nature") -> False
    if name == "linkedin":        # never reached
        results[name] = href ...
```

**That's why you got 13 Facebook links and 0 LinkedIn ones.** The pages weren't absent; the validator was rejecting every one.

Fixed: the validator accepts a handle or a URL, and all three strategies now store the composed URL through one helper. Strategies 2 and 3 would previously have stored a bare handle into a column that holds URLs, so those are corrected too.

## Verification

21 new tests, no browser launched. **Each fix was reverted in turn to confirm the tests actually catch it:**

| Reverted | Tests that failed |
|---|---|
| LinkedIn validator | 6 |
| `profile.php` pattern | 6 |
| page-wait change | 2 |

386 tests pass, ruff clean.

**Not verified:** no live scrape was run. The timeout fix can only be proven against real sites — that's the re-run below.

## Deliberately not touched

The 9 pre-existing Facebook values containing spaces, the `reel` Instagram handle, and the `TEST IMPORT CO` record. Those are data, not code, and they're yours to decide on.

Small but worth its own PR because it's a trap I walked into myself.

Git removes files that an incoming merge deletes **even when they're now gitignored**. So any clone still holding the tracked copy of `data/competitors_seed.json` loses it on the next `git pull`.

This happened on your machine immediately after merging #26 — `git pull` deleted the real seed file. I restored it from a backup taken earlier in the session and verified it: 77 records, 75 emails, sha256 matches. It's now correctly gitignored and won't be re-committed. Your `kinz-competitor-intelligence-BACKUP-2026-07-21` copy was never touched and also still has it.

Nothing was lost, but it would have been if I hadn't had that copy — so the README now says so before someone hits it on a second machine.

Also moves the `gh secret set COMPETITORS_SEED_JSON` instruction into the README rather than leaving it buried in #26's description, since the README is where you'd look when the Monday scrape reports three competitors.

Docs only, no code.

Implements your choice on backlog item 6: move the real seed data to an untracked file, commit a template.

## What changed

`data/competitors_seed.json` — 77 records naming real people with phone numbers and emails — is now **gitignored and local-only**. It is still on your disk, untouched.

Committed in its place: `data/competitors_seed.example.json`, three records with the identical key structure and placeholder contacts, so a fresh clone and CI still exercise `scripts/seed_from_json.py`.

The script falls back to the example when the real file is absent and says so loudly. Its success line now reports the file it actually read rather than the one it was asked for — otherwise the fallback is invisible.

Verified by moving the real file aside and running it:

```
⚠️  data/competitors_seed.json not found — falling back to data/competitors_seed.example.json.
    That file contains PLACEHOLDER contacts, not real ones.
✅ Seeded 3 competitors from data/competitors_seed.example.json
```

Real file restored byte-identical afterwards (sha256 checked).

## The part that nearly broke silently

`.github/workflows/scrape.yml` seeds from this file and then scrapes "competitors 1-25" and "26-49" **every Monday at 3am**.

Untracking it would have quietly reduced your weekly scrape to 3 fake companies pointing at `example.tn`. Nothing would have failed — the workflow would have gone green and collected almost nothing. I'd have handed you a working-looking scraper that had stopped scraping.

Both seeding steps now restore the real file from a repository secret, and emit a `::warning::` annotation if it's unset, so a misconfigured run is visible in the Actions UI rather than looking successful.

## One thing you need to do

**The secret is not set by this PR.** It's your data and setting it is yours to do:

```bash
gh secret set COMPETITORS_SEED_JSON < data/competitors_seed.json
```

Until then, Monday's scrape will warn and seed placeholders. That's the safe failure direction, but it does mean the scrape isn't collecting anything real until you run it.

## Caveat, recorded in the README

Untracking removes the file from future working trees, **not from history**. Anyone with repo access can still recover it from earlier commits. Removing it properly means rewriting history and force-pushing, which breaks every existing clone — worth doing only if this repo ever stops being private. I haven't done it, and wouldn't without you asking explicitly.

365 tests pass, ruff clean, workflow YAML parses.

This is the mechanism for *"a way to continuously improve the repo... test, check for code improvement, organize everything and repeat"*. Three files, no automation yet — scheduling comes next, once you've seen what a cycle produces.

## `CLAUDE.md`

What a cold session needs before touching anything. The useful half is the list of traps this repo has actually sprung, each tied to the PR that found it:

- `st.tabs` executes every tab body on every rerun (the root cause of the slowness)
- `st.rerun()` defaults to `scope="app"` — an earlier comment claimed the opposite and shaped a PR around it
- `st.cache_data` is process-global and leaked between tests
- `create_all()` creates tables, not columns
- `_coalesce` stringifies numbers; `blank_to_none` doesn't
- `init_db()` inside save helpers took exclusive SQLite locks

Plus the standing rules: never push to `main`, never commit credentials, the database isn't reproducible, measure before optimising and quote the number.

## `docs/IMPROVEMENTS.md`

The ranked backlog, seeded with real findings rather than generic advice.

Top item is extracting the four remaining save helpers, because doing exactly that to the fifth one (#23) turned up a data-loss bug that had been live for months. Same shape, no scrutiny yet.

It also records what was **Dropped** and why — `black`, Claude-in-GitHub-Actions, targeted cache invalidation — so those don't get re-proposed every few weeks by a session that wasn't there for the reasoning.

## `.claude/commands/improve.md`

One cycle: check open PRs and **stop at three**, sync, take the top item, work it, verify, ship, update the backlog, stop.

The throttle is the important part. Review is the bottleneck, not authorship, and a pile of unreviewed PRs is worse than none — it guarantees conflicts and means nothing is actually being looked at.

Two rules in it come directly from mistakes made in this repo:

- **Prove the test would have caught the bug** — reintroduce the old behaviour, watch it fail, restore. A test that only ever passed proves nothing.
- **Never claim a PR, a passing run, or a measurement that didn't happen.**

It also refuses to self-merge anything that touches a write path tests don't pin down, changes scraper behaviour, or needs a decision that's yours rather than mine.

## One thing I need from you

Backlog item 6: `data/competitors_seed.json` has **77 records with real contact details** committed to the repo. It's private, so this may be fine — but it's marked *"needs a decision from the repo owner, do not act on this unilaterally"* and the routine will keep skipping it until you say which way you want it. Options are leave as-is, move to an untracked file with a committed template, or scrub to placeholders and keep the real data local.

365 tests pass, ruff clean. No code changed in this PR.

## The fragment

The Outlets filters, map and editor are now wrapped in `st.fragment`. Typing in the search box or changing a governorate re-runs that block instead of all nine tab bodies. This is the tab you reported as slowest, and it was only safe to isolate once #23 covered the save helper inside it.

The KPI row stays outside the fragment deliberately — it summarises the whole table rather than the filtered view, so it should refresh on an app rerun, not a filter change.

**Not measured end-to-end.** `AppTest` reruns the whole script, so it cannot observe a fragment-scoped rerun; I have no honest number to quote. The mechanism is what Streamlit documents, and the saving is the eight other tab bodies not executing per keystroke. You will feel it in the search box.

## Two things that turned up, both bigger than the fragment

### 1. The smoke tests were not testing anything

The dashboard's loaders are `@st.cache_data(ttl=30)`. The cache is process-global and `AppTest` runs the app in the same process, but `_run_app()` never cleared it. So the empty frames cached by `test_app_runs_on_empty_database` were reused by every later test in the file.

That means these were all asserting against **no data**, despite their fixtures seeding it:

- `test_app_runs_with_data`
- `test_all_nine_tabs_render`
- `test_no_schema_drift_warning_on_current_schema`
- `test_no_load_failures_reported`

This is a hole in the safety net I built in Phase B, and I only found it because the new fragment test failed with "outlets fragment did not run" — the outlets widgets only exist on the non-empty branch.

`_run_app()` now clears the cache first. With real data flowing, `test_app_runs_with_data` immediately failed:

```
AssertionError: ['1 product(s) dropped more than 10%']
```

That is the price-drop banner working correctly — it uses `st.error` to get a red box, so a healthy app with a price drop in it emits one. Rather than widen the assertion to ignore all errors, `_unexpected_errors()` filters that one message by content so the check stays meaningful.

### 2. A comment I added in #22 was wrong

It claimed a save's `st.rerun()` inside a fragment would only refresh the fragment, and used that to justify not wrapping the save handlers. That is false:

```
scope : "app" or "fragment"
    If ``scope`` is ``"app"`` (default), the full app reruns.
```

`st.rerun()` reruns the whole app even from inside a fragment. Only the explicit `scope="fragment"` is fragment-local. I corrected the comment in place rather than deleting it, since the wrong version is what shaped #22's scope and that is worth leaving legible.

The underlying caution in #22 still stands on its own terms — the save logic genuinely was untested — but the technical reason I gave for it was not the real one.

## Also

The outlets empty-state still quoted 1–2 hours for a full Google Maps pass. The real figure is 8–12 hours, already corrected in the README, CONTEXT.md and the Word guide.

365 tests pass, ruff clean.

**Not measured end-to-end.** `AppTest` reruns the whole script, so it cannot observe a fragment-scoped rerun; I have no honest number to quote. The mechanism is what Streamlit documents, and the saving is the eight other tab bodies not executing per keystroke. You will feel it in the search box.

## Two things that turned up, both bigger than the fragment

### 1. The smoke tests were not testing anything

The dashboard's loaders are `@st.cache_data(ttl=30)`. The cache is process-global and `AppTest` runs the app in the same process, but `_run_app()` never cleared it. So the empty frames cached by `test_app_runs_on_empty_database` were reused by every later test in the file.

That means these were all asserting against **no data**, despite their fixtures seeding it:

- `test_app_runs_with_data`
- `test_all_nine_tabs_render`
- `test_no_schema_drift_warning_on_current_schema`
- `test_no_load_failures_reported`

This is a hole in the safety net I built in Phase B, and I only found it because the new fragment test failed with "outlets fragment did not run" - the outlets widgets only exist on the non-empty branch.

`_run_app()` now clears the cache first. With real data flowing, `test_app_runs_with_data` immediately failed:

```
AssertionError: ['1 product(s) dropped more than 10%']
```

That is the price-drop banner working correctly - it uses `st.error` to get a red box, so a healthy app with a price drop in it emits one. Rather than widen the assertion to ignore all errors, `_unexpected_errors()` filters that one message by content so the check stays meaningful.

### 2. A comment I added in #22 was wrong

It claimed a save's `st.rerun()` inside a fragment would only refresh the fragment, and used that to justify not wrapping the save handlers. That is false:

```
scope : "app" or "fragment"
    If ``scope`` is ``"app"`` (default), the full app reruns.
```

`st.rerun()` reruns the whole app even from inside a fragment. Only the explicit `scope="fragment"` is fragment-local. I corrected the comment in place rather than deleting it, since the wrong version is what shaped #22's scope and that is worth leaving legible.

The underlying caution in #22 still stands on its own terms - the save logic genuinely was untested - but the technical reason I gave for it was not the real one.

## Also

The outlets empty-state still quoted 1-2 hours for a full Google Maps pass. The real figure is 8-12 hours, already corrected in the README, the design notes and the Word guide.

365 tests pass, ruff clean.

## What this is

I set out to make the Outlets save logic testable so the remaining `st.fragment` work could proceed safely. Extracting it turned up a latent data-loss bug, so this PR is both.

## The bug

`save_parapharmacy_changes` ran every field through app.py's `_coalesce`, which returns `str(value).strip()`. `st.data_editor` hands numeric columns back as **floats**, so:

```
reviews_count 250 -> editor returns 250.0 -> _coalesce -> "250.0" -> int("250.0") -> ValueError
```

The `except (TypeError, ValueError)` around the cast swallowed it and wrote `NULL`.

**Effect:** opening the Outlets tab and pressing Save erased the review counts it had just displayed, for every row in the editor. Not only edited rows — every row goes through the update loop on each save.

The other save helpers were checked and are **not** affected: they call `float(val)` on the raw value and never route numerics through `_coalesce`.

## Has it already caused damage?

No. The live database has 3,578 outlets, of which 22 have a rating but no review count. All 22 are `source='Google Maps'` with `is_stockist`/`contacted`/`notes` unset, i.e. never touched by the editor — scrape gaps, not damage. The bug was latent.

## Changes

**`dashboard/saves.py`** (new) — `apply_parapharmacy_changes(db, edited_df, original_df)` takes an open session, returns `{"added", "updated", "deleted"}`, commits on success, rolls back and re-raises on failure. No Streamlit calls, so it is testable.

**`blank_to_none()`** replaces `_coalesce` on this path and returns values unchanged. Named differently on purpose — two functions called some variant of "coalesce" with different semantics in one package is precisely how this survived. `_coalesce` is untouched for the callers that still depend on its stringifying behaviour.

**`dashboard/app.py`** — `save_parapharmacy_changes` is now a thin wrapper owning `st.success` / `st.error` / cache clear / rerun. `st.rerun()` moved out of the `try` block.

**`tests/test_dashboard_saves.py`** — 25 tests: adds, edits, deletes, the pipeline fields (`is_stockist` / `contacted` / `notes`), NaN and blank handling, numeric casts, blank-row filtering, rows removed by another process, and the empty/None frames.

## Verification

The regression test was checked against the bug, not just run green — reinstating the old stringifying behaviour fails it:

```
FAILED test_float_review_count_survives_a_save
E   assert None == 250
    +  where None = <Parapharmacy Para Alpha>.reviews_count
```

364 tests pass, ruff clean.

## Why this ordering

Two of the tests guard things that are easy to get backwards and expensive to get wrong:

- `test_nothing_is_deleted_when_the_frames_match` — inverting the diff direction would wipe the table.
- `test_capped_view_does_not_delete_rows_outside_it` — the editor is capped and search-filtered, so `edited_df` is a subset. If deletions were computed against the whole table rather than `original_df`, saving a filtered view would delete everything off screen.

The Outlets table carries the sales pipeline, which the scrapers cannot regenerate. Wrapping that tab in `st.fragment` changes what a save's `st.rerun()` refreshes; that was not a change worth making over untested write logic. It is now unblocked.

Phase 3, **partially** — and I want to be explicit about what I deliberately left out.

## What's here

Dragging the alert threshold used to re-execute all nine tab bodies on every step, because `st.tabs` evaluates each one on every rerun regardless of which tab is visible. Wrapped in `@st.fragment`, a drag now re-runs only that block.

## What I did NOT do, and why

The plan also proposed fragments around the **outlets** and **products** filters. I'm not shipping those yet:

- the products tab contains **5** save/rerun calls, the outlets tab **3**
- the `save_*` helpers have **zero test coverage** (`grep` over `tests/`: 0 references)
- inside a fragment, a handler's `st.rerun()` only refreshes *the fragment* — so a save silently appears not to take effect elsewhere in the app unless every one is changed to `st.rerun(scope="app")`

That's a refactor of untested database-write paths with a failure mode that stays invisible until someone loses an edit. Not something to merge unreviewed.

The alerts block has none of that — nothing in it writes to the database or calls `st.rerun()` — so it's a clean win standing alone.

**The right order is: cover the save helpers with tests, then fragment the tabs that contain them.** That's the next piece of work, and it also closes the 23% `app.py` coverage gap flagged in #20.

- [x] Verified zero `st.rerun` / `save_*` / `cache_data.clear` calls inside the fragment

Phase 2 — the payload half of the dashboard slowness, and the Brave disconnect the code itself documented.

## Editors: three of nine were unbounded

The **outlets editor** was the only one with **neither a row cap nor a checkbox gate**: 3,578 rows × 14 columns with `num_rows="dynamic"`, rendered on every rerun whether or not anyone intended to edit. The file's own comment at `MAX_EDITOR_ROWS` records Brave dropping the connection around 200 rows.

It now uses the existing `cap_rows_for_editor()` helper and the same checkbox gate the competitors and products editors already had. Also capped the products editor (up to 1,905 rows) and price-history editor (1,789) — both gated but uncapped.

Two deliberate details:
- **Exporting stays outside the gate** — you shouldn't have to turn on edit mode to download a CSV.
- **The save button moved inside it**, since it references the editor's output and would otherwise raise `NameError` when editing is off. (Caught that while restructuring.)

## Outlet map

Collapsed by default and capped at 1,500 markers, chosen by review count so the busiest outlets survive. 3,578 markers with per-point hover data was ~414 KB of plot JSON per rerun — and an expander that defaults to open still builds and ships its contents.

The label states when it's capped rather than silently truncating: *"2,000 with GPS — showing the 1,500 most-reviewed"*.

## `.streamlit/config.toml` (new)

There was no config at all. Sets `maxMessageSize` to 50 MB (well above what this app needs, but low enough to fail loudly if something regresses into an unbounded payload), enables `fastReruns`, disables usage stats, pins the theme.

`.gitignore` previously excluded all of `.streamlit/`. Narrowed it so `config.toml` is shared while `secrets.toml` stays ignored — verified both directions with `git add --dry-run`.

## Test plan

- [x] `AppTest` against **2,000 synthetic outlets**: no exceptions, 0 errors
- [x] Edit gate renders; map reports the cap correctly and is collapsed
- [x] `edited_para` verified to be referenced only inside the gate (no `NameError` path)
- [x] `.streamlit/config.toml` addable, `secrets.toml` still blocked
- [x] `ruff check .` — All checks passed
- [x] `pytest tests/` — **339 passed**

Phase B — the safety net that makes everything after it reviewable.

The 311 existing tests covered the scrapers, PDF parser and API. **None touched `dashboard/app.py`** — the 2,400-line file every recent change has modified, and the one an automated improvement loop would touch. A broken import, a renamed column, or an exception inside any of the nine tabs would only have surfaced by opening a browser.

> **It found a real bug before it was finished.** The seeded fixture does `Parapharmacy(business_category=...)`, which raised `TypeError` — because the outlet classifier had never reached `main`. That became #19.

## `dashboard/analysis.py` (new)

`dashboard/app.py` executes top to bottom on import — page config, database loads, nine tab bodies — so nothing in it can be imported for testing.

Moved the two pure computations out: `compute_price_drops` and `select_plottable_products`, plus `PRICE_CHART_MAX_SERIES`. No Streamlit import, so tests run in milliseconds. These are exactly the two functions that were the dashboard's worst hot spots (4.4s and 1.3s per rerun before being rewritten), so they're the ones most worth pinning down.

## `tests/test_dashboard_smoke.py` — 5 tests, ~3.4s

`streamlit.testing.v1.AppTest` runs the real script in-process, no browser needed. Covers the empty database (what a new user hits first), the populated path, and all nine tabs being present.

Two are worth calling out: it asserts the dashboard reports **neither schema drift nor loader failures**. That schema check is a standing guard against the exact bug where a model gains a column with no matching migration entry — which has now happened twice.

## `tests/test_dashboard_analysis.py` — 19 tests, 0.5s

Boundary and correctness cases for the price-drop logic: exclusive threshold, increases ignored, **row order irrelevant** (the loader returns newest-first), intermediate prices ignored, zero baseline not dividing by zero, missing prices skipped, sort order, per-product independence, absent company column, negative threshold treated as magnitude.

## `tests/test_perf_budget.py` — 4 tests, 0.4s

Converts the Phase 1 speedups into regressions CI catches. Thresholds are ~10× the measured times so they catch an *algorithmic* regression without failing on a noisy runner, and one test asserts **scaling** rather than wall-clock.

**I verified these actually fail.** Reintroducing the old per-product loop and removing the single-reading filter produced:

```
AssertionError: price-drop computation took 1384ms over 2010 rows —
  expected well under 500ms. A per-product loop has probably crept back in.

AssertionError: 2000 products would be offered to the chart, expected 10 —
  the single-reading filter is not working.
```

## Coverage

Added `pytest-cov`, reported in CI, **not gated on a global percentage** — a floor pressures whoever is raising it into writing tests that execute lines without asserting anything, which is worse than no test.

| | coverage |
|---|---|
| `dashboard/analysis.py` | **100%** |
| `dashboard/app.py` | 23% |

**23% is the honest number and the remaining gap**: the smoke tests prove the app *runs*, but the `save_*` helpers are still uncovered. They need `st` mocked or a further extraction — worth doing before the improvement loop is allowed to touch them.

## Test plan

- [x] `pytest tests/` — **339 passed** (was 311)
- [x] `ruff check .` — All checks passed
- [x] Perf budgets verified to fail on an injected regression, then restored and green
- [x] Smoke tests pass against both an empty and a populated database

## Notes for reviewer

- Stacks on #19 (merged) — the fixture needs the `business_category` model column.
- No behaviour change to the dashboard: the extraction is move-only, with `app.py` importing what it previously defined.
